STATEMENT OF INTEREST
Amici Curiae (“Amici”) include a bipartisan group of 81 current and former 
state and local election officials and 19 local jurisdictions charged with the 
responsibility for administering elections, including federal elections. Amici hail from 
a diverse range of states and localities, including 27 states. Amici also include the 
Center for Election Innovation and Research (“CEIR”), which consists of election 
experts who support election officials’ work.1 Amici submit this brief in opposition to 
the pending application to stay the preliminary injunction issued by the United States 
District Court for the District of Massachusetts against portions of the final rule 
recently promulgated by the United States Postal Service (“USPS”), entitled “Ballot 
Mail for Federal Elections,” 91 Fed. Reg. 54966 (Aug. 26, 2026) (to be codified at 39 
C.F.R. pt. 111) (hereinafter the “Final Rule” or “Rule”).2
Given their roles and responsibilities, Amici have a strong interest in the fair 
and efficient administration of elections, in safeguarding the right to vote, and in 
protecting the constitutionally derived authority of states and localities to regulate 
elections within their borders. To carry out their duties, election officials develop 
policies and procedures for their offices, train staff and poll workers, educate voters, 
1 Pursuant to Supreme Court Rule 37.6, Amici state that no party or party’s counsel 
authored this brief in whole or in part, and no party or party’s counsel contributed 
money intended to fund preparation or submission of this brief. A list of all Amici is 
provided at Appendix A.
2 The district court enjoined the implementation and enforcement of certain 
provisions of the Final Rule only as to elections occurring on or before November 3, 
2026. See Appl. 2a, 47a-49a.

2
and respond to real-time constituent needs within their respective jurisdictions. Amici
election officials are also bound under the National Voter Registration Act (“NVRA”) 
to “promote the exercise of” the “fundamental right” to vote. 52 U.S.C. § 20501(a)(1)–
(2). Amici are unified in their commitment to ensuring that elections operate in 
accordance with state and federal law and that every eligible voter has an opportunity 
to cast a ballot.
As the front-line workers of election administration and election administration 
experts, Amici understand the practicalities of administering elections and are wellpositioned to explain the significant administrative problems and confusion 
introduced by the challenged USPS Final Rule. Based on their extensive experience 
and expertise, Amici write to offer the Court their first-hand perspective about the onthe-ground impact of the Final Rule, including the disastrous and immediate harms 
that the Rule would impose on election officials and their ongoing preparations for the 
upcoming November 2026 midterm elections if the district court’s injunction is not 
maintained.
INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
Preparing for a federal election is a massive undertaking, requiring many 
months, if not years, of advance planning and coordination among thousands of state 
and local election officials nationwide. And each step in that process—including 
recruiting and training election workers, communicating with voters, printing ballots, 
and ensuring that voters can cast their ballots, whether in-person or by mail—is 
critical to protecting the fundamental exercise of the franchise. Against that backdrop, 
the late-breaking USPS Final Rule—which was promulgated mere months before the

3
November 3, 2026 general midterm elections, and which mandates sweeping, costly, 
and burdensome changes to mail-in voting procedures—would prove disastrous for 
election officials and election administration. And it would seriously undermine the 
upcoming elections by depriving untold numbers of citizens of their ability to vote by 
mail, as permitted by state law.
Amici fully agree with Respondents’ legal argument that the challenged Final 
Rule is unconstitutional and unlawful many times over. It violates core constitutional 
separation-of-powers principles, contravenes multiple statutory limitations on the 
Postal Service’s authority, and is otherwise ultra vires. As the district court correctly 
found when enjoining it, the Rule marks an unprecedented and indefensible assertion 
of executive power in an area where USPS has neither expertise nor experience, let 
alone any lawful authority. See App. 25a-31a.
But Amici write primarily to highlight the grave practical consequences of the 
Rule, as well as the staggering logistical hurdles to implementing the Rule’s 
mandates—if it is even possible at all—in time for the rapidly approaching midterm 
elections. As of this filing, mail-in ballots are already being mailed out to voters in 
certain states. Other states and localities across the country have already designed, 
purchased, and printed their mail-in ballots and ballot envelopes. Yet the Final Rule 
would require scrapping those materials, and then re-designing and re-submitting 
mail-in ballot envelopes to USPS for approval, with no guarantee (and, indeed, 
essentially no plausible chance) that the agency would grant approval in time for 
jurisdictions to mail out their ballots to voters. The Rule would then require election 
officials to devote countless hours to inputting voter information into a brand-new, as-

4
yet-unfinished, and wholly untested federal portal—on which no election officials have 
yet received any training, and which is almost certain to be overloaded as soon as it 
comes online. If all that were not enough, the Rule would further require election 
officials to spend impossibly long periods of time waiting in person at local post offices 
while their jurisdictions’ mail-in ballot envelopes are scanned and verified by postal 
employees.
Every stage of this incomplete, untested, and poorly conceived process is ripe 
for errors. And the consequences would be grave: Millions of voters across the country 
rely on mail-in and absentee voting, and many of those voters would have no effective 
alternative if USPS precludes their ability to vote by mail. The district court 
independently reached the same conclusion on a developed evidentiary record. Most 
notably, the court found that immediate implementation of the Rule less than seventy 
days before the election “threatens disenfranchisement of millions of United States 
citizens,” while the record contained no evidence of fraudulent voting by mail to 
support this rushed implementation. App. 45a-46a. The insurmountable burdens 
imposed by the Final Rule would thus strike directly at the exercise of the 
fundamental right to vote and undermine public confidence in elections and election 
results.
Whatever the ultimate legality of the Final Rule, its novel requirements should 
not—and cannot responsibly—be allowed to go into effect on a mandatory basis for the 
elections less than two months away. Applicants’ assertion that the injunction itself 
“risks sowing confusion and chaos,” Appl. 5, turns reality on its head. On the contrary, 
it is USPS’s eleventh-hour imposition of a brand-new federal regime that would

5
disrupt settled procedures for mail-in ballots and introduce chaos into the election 
process already underway.
With mail-in voting having already begun, and with Respondents having 
satisfied every legal requirement for the order issued by the district court below, this 
Court should deny Applicants’ requested stay, preserve the settled procedures on 
which election officials and voters are relying, and avoid injecting into the November 
elections the chaos and risk of disenfranchisement that mandatory implementation of 
the Final Rule would create at this late stage.
ARGUMENT
I. A Stay Would Change the Rules of the Road After Election Officials 
Have Already Put Them Into Operation.
The demands and resulting impacts of implementing the Final Rule would be 
felt most acutely at the state and local levels, where elections are administered. Given 
the timelines mandated by the Rule itself and by other state and federal laws, 
combined with all of the administrative steps required by the Rule and by election 
administration generally, it is Amici’s considered view that it would be extremely
difficult if not impossible for election officials to implement the sweeping changes 
mandated in the Final Rule in time for the rapidly approaching November 3, 2026 
general midterm elections. Indeed, if the Final Rule is permitted to take effect for
those upcoming elections, the inevitable result would be widespread chaos and 
confusion and, ultimately, the disenfranchisement of significant numbers of voters 
who lawfully rely on voting by mail.
“[R]unning a statewide election is a complicated endeavor,” requiring 
“thousands of state and local officials and volunteers [to] participate in a massive

6
coordinated effort to implement the lawmakers’ policy choices on the ground before 
and during the election,” and requiring “at every step, state and local officials [to] 
communicate to voters how, when, and where they may cast their ballots through inperson voting on election day, absentee voting, or early voting.” Democratic Nat’l 
Comm. v. Wis. State Legislature, 141 S. Ct. 28, 31 (2020) (Kavanaugh, J., concurring 
in denial of application to vacate stay). Accordingly, the “Court’s precedents recognize 
a basic tenet of election law: When an election is close at hand, the rules of the road 
should be clear and settled.” Id.; see also Merrill v. Milligan, 142 S. Ct. 879, 880 (2022)
(Kavanaugh, J., concurring in grant of applications for stay) (acknowledging that 
“state and local election officials need substantial time to plan for elections” because 
“[r]unning elections state-wide is extraordinarily complicated and difficult . . . and 
pose[s] significant logistical challenges”).
USPS’s Final Rule, however, wholly upends the existing rules regarding voting 
by mail with less than two months remaining before the nationwide elections on 
November 3, 2026. Meanwhile, as Amici know from their personal experiences, 
preparations for the upcoming midterm elections, including those for voting by mail, 
have been well underway in states and localities across the country for many months. 
Yet the Final Rule threatens to derail those efforts at the last minute, causing 
incalculable harm to election administration, election officials, and voters alike.
Election officials like Amici are actively engaged in both administering 
primary elections (which are still set to occur in early- to mid-September 2026 in

7
several states3) while also preparing for the November 2026 general elections right 
now. This work involves a near-constant stream of critical and time-sensitive tasks 
required to administer safe, efficient, and fair elections. Those tasks include 
recruiting, training, and coordinating with election workers and volunteers; working 
with third-party vendors and contractors; establishing and promulgating guidance 
and rules for election administration; engaging in voter education; processing voter 
registrations and handling voter registration challenges; preparing and printing 
ballots and ballot envelopes; finalizing polling sites and ballot dropbox locations; and 
preparing, programming, and testing voting machines and tabulation equipment. 
Moreover, although Election Day itself is November 3, 2026, early voting begins in 
October 2026 for a majority of states and starts as early as mid-September (e.g., 
September 18, 19, or 24, 2026) in a handful of states.4 To put it mildly, election 
officials across the country, including Amici, are incredibly busy with election 
preparation tasks that are already well underway. See also App. 42a-43a.
As particularly relevant to the significant changes mandated in USPS’s Final 
Rule, states and localities nationwide have already begun preparations in earnest for 
mail-in balloting and absentee voting by mail, in accordance with their respective 
states’ laws. Each state’s laws impose different requirements and set different 
deadlines for voting by mail, with September 4, 2026 being the earliest date on which 
3 See 2026 Primary Elections by State and Territory, Fed. Voting Assistance Program, 
https://perma.cc/ED3Q-C2AC; 2026 State Primary Election Dates, Nat’l Conf. of State 
Legislatures (May 27, 2026), https://perma.cc/XY47-8Y6R. 
4 See Early Voting Dates, 2026, Ballotpedia, https://perma.cc/J9H5-RY57.

8
ballots were mailed out in at least one state, and October 16, 2026 being the latest 
date on which ballots may be mailed out in other states.5 Meanwhile, under the 
Uniformed and Overseas Citizens Absentee Voting Act (“UOCAVA”), as amended by 
the Military and Overseas Voter Empowerment (“MOVE”) Act, Pub. L. No. 111-84 
§ 579(a)(1)(C), 123 Stat. 2190, 2322 (2009), federal law mandates that election 
officials must mail absentee ballots to overseas and military voters no later than 
September 19, 2026. See 52 U.S.C. § 20302(a)(8)(A) (requiring requested ballots to be 
mailed out 45 days in advance of a federal election).6
In light of these looming deadlines—and deadlines that have already passed
in some states—most jurisdictions have already designed and placed orders for their 
mail-in ballots and envelopes, and many jurisdictions have in fact already printed 
those envelopes and/or received them from third-party vendors. As explained in 
greater detail below, canceling those pending orders or discarding already-purchased 
envelopes at this late date would not only result in dramatically increased costs for 
rush-printing services but would render it exceedingly difficult, if not impossible, for 
jurisdictions to re-design, re-print, and mail out ballots in time to comply with their 
respective states’ statutory deadlines.
5 See Table 7: When States Mail Out Absentee/Mail Ballots, Nat’l Conf. of State Leg.,
https://perma.cc/4XZE-GHH7 (listing deadlines for mailing out absentee/mail-in 
ballots by state, with North Carolina and Delaware falling at the beginning of the 
window and Washington and Colorado falling at the later end of the window).
6 Although Amici recognize that the Final Rule does not itself cover UOCAVA ballots, 
the UOCAVA deadline informs election officials’ preparations of mail-in ballots, and 
it helps to explain why jurisdictions have already begun preparing, ordering, and 
printing such ballots and ballot envelopes.

9
Moreover, jurisdictions nationwide have already set their budgets for 
administering the upcoming midterm elections. Funds have been appropriated and, 
in many cases, allocated and spent on other critical election-related infrastructure 
and materials. Yet despite requiring costly and administratively burdensome 
changes, all on a moment’s notice, the Final Rule does not provide any financial 
support whatsoever to states and localities to implement the Rule’s mandates. 
Further compounding these problems, the Final Rule comes at a time when local 
election offices throughout the country are already facing severe staffing challenges. 
Since the 2020 election, there has been well-documented turnover in local election 
officials, who have faced increased threats to their safety and recently heightened 
risks of federal criminal investigation and prosecution.7 This has led to reductions in 
the overall number of staff and the number of staff with long-term experience. The 
extraordinarily compressed deadlines that the Final Rule mandates for the upcoming 
midterm elections would thus create intractable operational problems for state and 
local election officials, who would be required to implement and comply with the 
Rule’s mandates regarding mail-in voting on impossible timelines, with limited 
personnel and limited financial flexibility.
7 See, e.g., New Report Reveals Alarming Election Official Turnover and Offers 
Solutions, Issue One (Feb. 3, 2026), https://perma.cc/5Q7K-7GHE; Local Election 
Officials Survey 3, Brennan Ctr. for Just. (Apr. 13, 2026), https://perma.cc/C49KEC2S (noting that thirty-two percent of local election officials surveyed reported 
experiencing threats, harassment, or abuse because of their job, while fifty-two 
percent reported concern for the safety of their colleagues); Kate Brumback, Justice 
Department Seeks the Names of 2020 Election Workers in Georgia’s Fulton County, 
AP (May 5, 2026), https://perma.cc/5K73-58F7.

10
In short, and as explained in further detail below, the changes marked by the 
Final Rule simply come too late and are too burdensome to be workable for the 
upcoming November 2026 general elections. It would be exceedingly difficult, if not 
impossible, for Amici and their fellow election officials to implement those changes 
on this timetable while also performing all the work necessary to administer free and 
fair elections.
II. The Balance of Equities and Public Interest Overwhelmingly Favor 
Denying a Stay of the Preliminary Injunction.
The Final Rule imposes onerous new requirements for mail-in voting, with the 
burdens of its implementation falling on state and local election officials. Unlike the 
Executive Order previously before this Court, the Final Rule unquestionably imposes
concrete demands on state and local election officials. Granting a stay of the district 
court’s existing injunction would thus require those officials to meet those demands
at the expense of the critical work already underway to administer the November 
elections. That distinction matters to the equities: This Court previously concluded 
that a stay of the previous preliminary injunction would not “concretely harm” the 
States precisely because the Executive Order “makes no demand” of them. Trump v. 
California, No. 25A124, slip op., at 10 (U.S. Aug. 24, 2026). The Final Rule does. 
Applicants do not even contest this. Instead, they recast the demands as “modest 
conditions” on the acceptance of federal-election ballot mailings, Appl. at 22, but this 
characterization is belied by both the record below and the extensive experience of 
Amici, who would be required to implement the new requirements on the ground.
The Rule dramatically overhauls the existing system, under which states have 
long relied on USPS to neutrally and expeditiously mail out and then return voters’

11
mail-in and absentee ballots. And it replaces that status quo with a system under 
which USPS would now refuse to transmit ballots by mail unless states scrupulously 
adhere to all the Rule’s new requirements. But each new step of the process outlined 
in the Final Rule would introduce delay, confusion, and intolerable risks of errors, all 
while voters’ fundamental right to vote hangs in the balance.
For a state to comply with the Final Rule, it must first ensure that its outbound 
and return ballot envelopes comply with new design requirements, including the 
incorporation of Intelligent Mail barcodes, and it must submit its envelope designs to 
USPS for review and approval. 91 Fed. Reg. at 54990-91. After obtaining approval of 
the ballot envelope and return envelope designs, state or local election officials must 
then input each voter’s information into a USPS-run electronic Federal Ballot Mail 
Portal. 91 Fed. Reg. at 54991. Notably, the Final Rule provides no timeline for USPS’s 
approval of ballot envelopes, but it nonetheless precludes election officials from 
uploading voter information into the Portal until USPS first approves the envelope 
designs, including the required Intelligent Mail barcodes. Id. And where state or local 
election officials do not obtain advance envelope approval from USPS, or do not 
successfully upload all voter information into the USPS Portal, the agency would not 
mail that state’s ballots to voters. Id.
Based on Amici’s experience, and as outlined more specifically below, 
attempting to comply with each of these new requirements in advance of the 
upcoming November 2026 elections would require a significant investment of time 
and resources, which many jurisdictions simply do not have to spare at this point in 
the electoral cycle. In addition, the compounding delays and inevitable errors

12
introduced throughout the process would almost certainly result in a significant 
number of voters being unable to effectively cast their votes by mail. Those 
consequences would fall especially heavily on voters who rely on mail-in voting 
because of age, disability, or temporary residence, and whom state law permits to 
vote by mail.
A. The Final Rule’s mandates for re-designing ballot envelopes 
would be financially costly and likely cannot be accomplished 
in time for the November 2026 elections.
The Final Rule adopts rigid design specifications for all outbound and return 
envelopes for absentee and mail-in ballots for federal elections. See 91 Fed. Reg. at 
54990–91. Each envelope must include the “official Election Mail logo,” be 
“automation compatible,” and bear “the voter’s unique [Intelligent Mail barcode].” Id.
To comply with these demands, many state and local election officials would be 
required to re-design and even re-print their ballot envelopes. As explained above, 
many jurisdictions have already ordered their ballot envelopes, and some have 
already printed, received, or even mailed those envelopes. The need to discard those 
old envelopes and re-design and re-print new ones in advance of the November 2026 
elections would impose significant costs, including for rush printing jobs by thirdparty vendors equipped to handle these new technical requirements on short notice.
The mandated changes regarding envelope design would be felt at every level 
of election administration. Most states do not have a single design for mail-ballot 
envelopes. Counties and localities in a single state may use different voting machines 
and different types and sizes of ballots, requiring different ballot and envelope 
designs. Changing these processes to comply with the Final Rule’s mandates would

13
be a major undertaking, requiring significant time and monetary resources—burdens 
which would inevitably fall on state and local election officials. Indeed, under the 
Final Rule, state and local election officials are “responsible for barcode creation” “as
well as envelope design and printing for all ballot mail.” Id. at 54991. But the Final 
Rule provides no funding for implementing these major changes, nor sufficient time 
for their completion before the Rule would make compliance a condition of 
transmitting ballots to voters.
For example, the requirement that every jurisdiction use Intelligent Mail 
barcodes on each outbound and return envelope creates onerous new obligations that 
would be costly and difficult—if not impossible—for election officials to follow, 
particularly in time for the upcoming midterm elections. This would especially impact 
rural communities that do not currently have the technology to produce these 
barcodes8 and large urban areas that must process high volumes of election mail. 
USPS’s suggestion that it offers “free” tools for generating Intelligent Mail barcodes 
provides an incomplete solution. See 91 Fed. Reg. at 54979. USPS’s tool is only 
available for mailings with fewer than 50,000 pieces of mail.9 Thus, the largest 
counties in states across the nation, including in Arizona, Colorado, and Washington,
would not be able to use this USPS tool for their election mail. And, according to 
8 See Dion Nissenbaum et al., USPS Proposal to Carry Out Trump’s Executive Order 
Could Create New Barriers to Mail Voting, VOTEBEAT (May 29, 2026), 
https://perma.cc/8TV4-MW5K.
9 See USPS, Intelligent Mail® for Small Business (IMsb) Fact Sheet (June 1, 2023), 
https://perma.cc/H744-ZQKD.

14
Arizona’s top election official, not a single one of Arizona’s counties includes
Intelligent Mail barcodes on return-ballot envelopes, which have already been 
printed.10 Exacerbating the unexpected expense of this requirement, many 
jurisdictions would have to move from in-house printing to a rush order submitted to 
a commercial mail vendor in hopes of printing envelopes in time for the November 3, 
2026 elections.
Moreover, USPS itself acknowledges that there are currently technical 
impediments that would prevent the creation of Intelligent Mail barcodes for certain 
voters, such as when a voter’s address cannot be verified using Delivery Point 
Verification, which can often miss certain non-traditional mailing addresses (e.g., 
tribal addresses, college dormitory addresses, and nursing-home addresses). See 91 
Fed. Reg. at 54979-80. While USPS “anticipates” that it will make modifications to 
this tool, it provides no timeline for these changes. Id. at 54979. Typically, USPS 
would spend at least a year implementing a new system like the verification process 
the Final Rule outlines. It would hold a conference for all impacted jurisdictions and 
provide trainings for those required to interact with the system.11 But none of that 
has happened for the new changes introduced by the Final Rule. As of the date of this 
filing, and after ballots have already been printed in many jurisdictions, and already 
mailed in some, election officials still have not received comprehensive guidance or 
10 Decl. Arizona Secretary of State Adrian Fontes ¶ 24(b), California v. USPS, No. 
1:26-cv-13917-IT (D. Mass Aug. 26, 2026), Dkt. No. 4-5 (hereinafter California D. Ct.).
11 Eric Katz, Postal Officials Say Trump’s Mail-Ballot Push Will Create Widespread 
Errors, NOTUS (Aug. 27, 2026), https://perma.cc/V56K-PAS5.

15
training on the Rule’s new requirements.12 This extraordinarily rushed 
implementation is bound to cause significant chaos and delays for election officials 
and, ultimately, for the voters whom they serve.13
In addition to the time and resources that merely printing the Intelligent Mail 
barcodes would require, the Final Rule also introduces exorbitant time demands and 
delays into the process of mailing ballots. Federal-ballot mailers would each need to 
be segregated from, for example, UOCAVA ballots and state-election-only ballots, 
neither of which are subject to the Final Rule, and then individually scanned and 
processed in-person at a local post office location. See 91 Fed. Reg. at 54981. This 
scanning and verification process alone would likely take more time than state and 
local election officials have to spare. Even if USPS employees physically scan the 
mail-in ballot envelopes for verification, state and local election officials like Amici
must “remain” at the “postal retail location during the verification process.” Id.
(emphasis added). An example using USPS’s own estimates illustrates the 
unworkable nature of the Final Rule’s demands. USPS estimates that scanning each 
of these envelope barcodes generally takes “less than a minute per mailpiece.” Id. If 
each scan approached USPS’s stated upper-end estimate, scanning Colorado’s more 
12 Indeed, Amici election officials in Pennsylvania report that USPS scheduled three 
training sessions on Intelligent Mail barcodes for September 1, 2, and 3, 2026, only 
to cancel all three sessions without explanation.
13 Amici are also concerned that the Final Rule’s new, untested system could 
inadvertently sweep in other time-sensitive election mailings bearing the Official 
Election Mail logo, potentially delaying or blocking critical communications to voters. 
USPS instructs election officials to use that logo not only for ballots, but also for voterregistration cards, absentee applications, polling-place notifications, and other 
election mail. See USPS, Election Mail, https://perma.cc/F8K3-VTPA.

16
than four million mail ballots would require more than 66,000 worker-hours. In their 
Application, USPS invokes the Rule’s separate assertion that verification of even 
“larger mailings” should take only “a few hours.” Appl. 32. But neither the Rule nor 
USPS explains how that assertion squares with USPS’s own per-mailpiece estimate, 
much less identifies any factual basis for it. With thousands of ballots arriving at a 
time and millions upon millions of ballots across the country, the inevitable delays 
would place an unworkable demand on worker hours that state and local election 
officials cannot afford—particularly during the extraordinarily busy final weeks 
leading up to a major election.
B. State and local election officials must use a USPS Portal that is 
not yet operational and for which they have not been trained.
If the Final Rule’s burdens associated with the envelope re-designs were not 
enough to justify preserving the district court’s order (they are), the further burdens 
on state and local election officials imposed by the Final Rule are. Before any ballots 
can be mailed out under the Final Rule, state and local election officials like Amici
must enter voter information into USPS’s Federal Ballot Mail Portal—an as-yetunavailable system on which no election officials have been trained. The chief election 
official of each state would be charged with authorizing users within their state to 
access this new Federal Ballot Mail Portal. See 91 Fed. Reg. at 54991. Local election 
officials like Amici would then be required to use that Portal to notify USPS of 
individuals to whom they plan to mail a ballot, including the unique barcodes 
associated with the outbound mailings and return ballots assigned to each voter. Id.
This information would be compiled to create the state’s “Mail-In and Absentee

17
Participation List.” Id.
But the Portal that election officials must use to comply with the Final Rule 
does not even exist in operational form. Just days ago, USPS acknowledged that it 
was still “mak[ing] refinements” to it and could offer no date certain for its 
availability, stating merely that it “anticipate[d] being in a position” to make the 
Portal available “by sometime next week.” California D. Ct. Dkt. No. 150-1 ¶ 3. With 
the election less than 60 days away, ballots already being mailed in some states, and 
the Portal’s technical specifications still unpublished, that tentative prediction leaves 
election officials with the prospect of having to implement an entirely new system on 
an uncertain date, potentially after they have already begun mailing ballots under 
existing procedures.
To input all of this information into this yet-to-be-released Portal, state and 
local election officials would be required to stand up wholly new procedures and train 
staff to input information to form the basis of the state-specific Mail-In and Absentee 
Participation Lists mandated by the Final Rule. Yet while the Final Rule demands 
that state and local election officials “must” provide the information for the Mail-In 
and Absentee Participation Lists “at least 30 days before the date of the federal 
election” “or by the date on which mail-in or absentee ballots may begin to be mailed 
under state law,” 91 Fed. Reg. at 54991, that deadline is now literally impossible to 
meet in many jurisdictions. North Carolina began mailing ballots on September 4,

18
2026,14 and numerous other States will do so within days or weeks. These timelines 
place election officials like Amici in an impossible position, and—if faced with a stay
of the district court’s injunction by this Court—would require them to begin diverting 
resources to comply with these new mandates before USPS has even provided a 
platform for inputting this information.
Elevating concerns further, on September 1, 2026, Senator Richard 
Blumenthal made public an anonymous whistleblower report from a federal official 
with direct knowledge of the Rule (the “Whistleblower Report”), which describes the 
rushed implementation of USPS’s system for verifying and transporting mail-in 
ballots.15 The whistleblower explicitly warned that “[e]lection officials will be 
responsible for reconciling issues” within the newly imposed regime, for which the 
“opportunity for error and other failures . . . is high.” Id. ¶¶ 3, 24. Additionally, and 
even more concerningly, USPS has adopted a “zero percent failure rate,” meaning 
that when USPS clerks scan batches of ballots to confirm that they match the 
information in the Federal Ballot Mail Portal, an issue with even one of the ballots 
will result in USPS returning the entire batch of ballots to the state or local 
jurisdiction without mailing them. Id. ¶¶ 26–30. And because a single batch may 
contain tens of thousands of ballots, one mismatch or scanning error could result in

Them, N.Y. Times (Sept. 4, 2026), https://perma.cc/BW5K-5HM7.
15 Anonymous Whistleblower Disclosure, Re: USPS Rushed Implementation of New 
and Untested IT Systems Threatens U.S. Ballot Mail Delivery, Whistleblower Aid 
(Aug. 30, 2026), https://perma.cc/Z3Z4-QD2A.

19
tens of thousands of otherwise valid ballots being rejected and returned to election 
officials rather than mailed to voters. That USPS expects to implement this entirely 
new system without adding personnel only compounds the risk of widespread 
operational failures. See 91 Fed. Reg. at 54986. Multiple USPS officials have 
reportedly described the development of this process—a process that relies on state 
and local election officials like Amici to fix system errors—as a “s**t show.”
Whistleblower Report ¶ 19 (citation modified).
The whistleblower’s grave concerns are consistent with other independent 
reporting. A longtime USPS executive who was “personally responsible for developing 
the network technology the agency would need to carry out its rule” predicted that 
the Portal is likely to suffer a 20% to 30% error rate, which “would be a disaster.”16
The burdens of implementing the Final Rule—and of addressing the 
consequences when its requirements cannot be met under the unrealistic timeframes 
imposed—fall squarely on state and local election officials like Amici. In many 
jurisdictions, election officials would be required to input data into the Portal 
manually (and likely even on an individual voter-by-voter basis). This is because 
states’ and localities’ existing data storage systems are unlikely to be compatible with 
the Portal (e.g., because many jurisdictions’ databases do not include fields that can 
capture information about the Intelligent Mail barcodes that must be submitted into 
the Portal). Nor can jurisdictions necessarily solve those problems by simply 
16 Eric Katz, Postal Officials Say Trump’s Mail-Ballot Push Will Create Widespread 
Errors, NOTUS (Aug. 27, 2026), https://perma.cc/V56K-PAS5.

20
purchasing new equipment or software on the timeline the Final Rule imposes, given 
the competitive and time-consuming procurement rules applicable in many 
jurisdictions.
Even if the Portal were operational and election officials could overcome these 
implementation hurdles, it would still be extremely time-consuming and practically 
infeasible to satisfy the Portal’s data-entry requirements for the November elections. 
Election officials would need to update the Portal data nearly daily as voters move, 
new voters register, or voters request mail-in ballots, including replacement ballots. 
Voter rolls are updated until the very last day that a jurisdiction can mail ballots, 
which in some jurisdictions is as close as four days before Election Day. The Final 
Rule would thus require election officials to continually update the Portal during 
precisely the period when they are focused on the other critical statutory and 
administrative duties necessary to administer the midterm elections.
Critically, election officials cannot simply rush the transfer of sensitive voter 
information into a brand-new and untested federal system when errors could 
implicate not only voters’ privacy, but their ability to receive and cast a ballot. Indeed, 
the Final Rule expressly states that outbound mailings that do not comply with the 
USPS Portal enrollment requirements “will not be accepted and will be returned.” 91 
Fed. Reg. at 54991. Thus, seemingly any error—regardless of how minor—would 
result in a ballot not being mailed to a voter. The Final Rule provides no guidance on 
how errors in Portal submissions or compiled Mail-In and Absentee Participation 
Lists would be identified and addressed, or how long that process would take. 
Furthermore, USPS has also provided no guidance as to how election officials can

21
submit information into the Portal while still complying with their state’s laws 
regarding privacy and confidentiality of voter data.17
Accordingly, the district court’s injunction against the Final Rule was an 
appropriate response to the immediate, here-and-now harms the Rule and its rushed 
implementation impose. And the injunction is narrowly calibrated to those harms: It 
suspends only mandatory implementation for the November 3, 2026 midterm
elections, while leaving implementation for later elections untouched.18
C. The Final Rule risks undermining state and local election 
officials’ efforts to promote voter confidence and participation 
in elections.
Election officials also play an important role in promoting voter confidence and 
increasing voter participation. Because the Final Rule imposes significant changes 
immediately preceding nationwide elections, election officials like Amici are 
struggling to prepare communications and trainings for election workers and the 
public to assuage confusion or concerns. These issues include how the Mail-in and 
Absentee Participation Lists would be used, how USPS would address or resolve

22
errors on those lists, and how registered voters can assure that they receive their 
mail-in or absentee ballot and can then confidently return it. To meet these growing 
concerns about the November 2026 midterm elections, state and local election 
officials already need to devote time and resources to voter education regarding the 
Final Rule’s changes. The price for these sorts of educational campaigns is 
substantial. These are expenditures for which jurisdictions have not accounted and 
for which the federal government has offered no support. Yet they are critical to 
assuring that state and local election officials can administer free and fair elections 
in which voters can trust this November.
Finally, the many uncertainties posed by the Rule would undermine election 
officials’ ability to assure voters that their votes will count. Because USPS will refuse 
to deliver ballots if a state does not comply with the Final Rule—including because of 
inadvertent errors in data entry into the Portal, problems with the Intelligent Mail 
barcodes on the ballot envelopes, or otherwise—USPS would end up refusing to 
transmit ballots for some citizens who are in fact properly registered to vote, and who 
are entitled to vote by mail under their state’s laws. And because election officials 
cannot predict in advance which ballots USPS may disallow, they would not be able 
to effectively counsel voters about how to ensure that they are able to successfully 
vote by mail. Furthermore, the Rule’s complicated requirements would likely lead 
some eligible voters to misunderstand whether they are able to use a mail-in ballot 
at all, and it may even lead some eligible voters to conclude that the added 
requirements make voting too confusing to be worthwhile. This runs directly counter

23
to election officials’ mandate to “promote the exercise of” the “fundamental right” to 
vote. 52 U.S.C. § 20501(a)(1)–(2).
III. The Final Rule exists within the context of the threatened 
prosecution of state and local election officials, and it would thus 
further discourage election officials and volunteers from serving.
The Final Rule imposes upon state and local election officials, including Amici, 
demands that are impossible to meet—all the while threatening them, through the 
Executive Order that precipitated the Final Rule, with federal criminal prosecution. 
Exec. Order No. 14399, 91 Fed. Reg. 17125 (Mar. 31, 2026), https://perma.cc/NY6VKJV3 (hereinafter “EO”). USPS has made clear that the primary purpose of the 
Federal Ballot Mail Portal and the Mail-in and Absentee Participation Lists is to 
“provide valuable insight” into mail-in voting for federal law enforcement, specifically 
through disclosing “a list of individuals to whom states planned to mail a ballot (and 
who may potentially use the mail to vote), along with the associated barcode data,” 
which in turn can purportedly be used to “identify potentially anomalous incidents 
that may merit further investigation.” 91 Fed. Reg. at 54980, 54982. This all comes 
in the context of an EO directing federal agencies to prioritize the investigation and 
prosecution “of State and local officials . . . who issue Federal ballots to individuals 
not eligible to vote in a Federal election.” EO § 2(b); see also id. § 5 (providing that 
“State or local election officials . . . [and] individuals involved in the administration 
of Federal elections; or public [] entities engaged in the printing, production,

24
shipment, or distribution of ballots may be referred to the Department of Justice for 
consideration of investigation or charges under” various federal criminal laws).19
These baseless legal threats have already harmed ongoing election 
preparations, including by deterring staff, volunteers, and contractors from agreeing 
to assist in election administration. Layering onto these threats the additional 
onerous requirements of the Final Rule—which mandates multiple new steps for the 
mail-in voting process, each of which introduces additional possibilities for 
inadvertent errors—would only further depress recruitment and retention efforts for 
both election officials and election volunteers alike.
Amici understand that the Executive Branch has claimed that these measures 
are justified because there is widespread fraud supposedly allowing non-citizens to 
vote. But election officials carefully follow state and federal law, adopting strict 
processes to ensure that only eligible voters can cast a ballot. As a result, in Amici’s 
experience—and as confirmed by numerous independent research studies—noncitizen voting is vanishingly rare.20 Amici are likewise aware that the EO limits its 
directives to “appropriate” prosecutions “consistent with applicable law.” EO §§ 2(b), 
7(b). But those qualifications provide little practical reassurance to election officials

Monnin, DOJ Issues Nationwide Threat to Prosecute Local Election Officials, NOTUS
(July 8, 2026), https://perma.cc/MQ69-NGGY.
20 See Claims of Noncitizen Registration or Voting: Analysis and Tracker, Ctr. for

25
being required, on an extraordinarily compressed timeline, to navigate a brand-new 
federal regime that creates numerous opportunities for inadvertent error. In Amici’s 
experience, the prospect of federal investigation or prosecution—even if ultimately 
determined to be unwarranted—has a chilling effect on the employees, volunteers, 
and contractors on whom election offices depend, especially when coupled with the 
uncertainty created by a new and untested mandatory federal regime. Amici, and 
other officials like them, cannot effectively do their jobs under such conditions.
* * *
In short, it is far too late in the election cycle to introduce such dramatic and 
unwarranted changes to the mail-in voting process. The district court’s order leaves 
election officials to administer the upcoming elections under the procedures already 
in place; this Court should not disrupt those procedures at this late stage by granting 
a stay.
CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, the Court should deny the application for a stay of
the district court’s injunction.
